card_quote: Default disposition: 'I've heard all this before.' Expects recycled QI material and has complained about errors and missing citations in fact books. / What would register with him: obscure or genuinely disputed cases, sources.
how_read: Read the front matter and the 'how this book was checked' note first with some suspicion. Went through Rounds 1 to 4 in order with a pen, flicked through Round 5, read the physics round carefully, dipped into Round 8 for Fermat and the toast, and read Round 9 because it is science history. Did not bother with Round 10 beyond the contents.

w1_best.why: Forty mice, shock strength and no measurement of arousal. The textbook curve is Hebb's, not Yerkes and Dodson's. I did not know that.
Twenty-six blacks at Monte Carlo traced back to a 1959 book, with the blog author who couldn't find it earlier. A genuinely unsettled one.
Fisher on Mendel is the kind of open question I'd actually want to read about.
The 1919 eclipse with the blurred plates. It admits the handling was contested and that the result has survived. Honest.
Hooke publishing the spring law as an anagram. New to me, and short.

w1_flat.why: Archimedes in the bath. Everyone knows it's an anecdote.
Einstein's Nobel was not for relativity. Pub-quiz staple.
Napoleon and malice and stupidity, a repeat of the Hanlon page.
Sink drain direction. Known to anyone who has done any physics.
The goldfish page. Written like a parody of a paper, and no real references.

w1_review.headline: Competent myth roundup, though I knew a third of it
w1_review.body: The better entries (Yerkes-Dodson, Monte Carlo, the 1919 plates) do show where a story comes from, and the book is willing to say DISPUTED. But the entries follow one template, the sources are often Wikipedia or a blog, and at least two pages (the Franklin kite and the goldfish) look unedited and contradict the claim that everything was checked. Bottom line: fine for a non-scientist's stocking, not for anyone who reads footnotes.

w2_review_first: It is QI with a scoring table. Most of what I checked from memory was about right, and a few entries taught me something, but the layout is repetitive and a couple of pages look like they escaped without being proofread. I'd not push it on a friend who cares about accuracy.

w2_lost.why: Hanlon, then Napoleon, then the same history in different words.
The goldfish page. I stopped taking the book's checking seriously after that.
Round 2 generally. Quotes with the wrong owner get samey after the fourth.

w2_read_aloud.why: Hot water freezing faster. At a table it will cause an actual argument, and the answer is honestly open.
Toast landing butter-side down turns out to have a physics paper. Good surprise.
The anagram is short and odd enough to read out in one go.
Fermat's margin, and that he probably had no proof, is a good deflation.
The cat was meant as an objection, not a claim. People get this backwards.

w2_cut.why: The Franklin page, which says TRUE and then says the opposite and is not even in the contents.
The goldfish entry, which reads as another author wrote it and cites 'various laboratory studies'.
A second Wald entry to say the first thing again.

w2_book2: More pages that look unproofed, Wikipedia and blogs as the sources, and more myths I already know.
